recent_developments.text: AMD launched MI300 for AI training workloads in June 2023 and is competing with NVIDIA for market share.
In June 2026 AMD announced the acquisition of MEXT, whose predictive-memory technology is designed to make flash behave more like DRAM and cut data center memory cost.
AMD launched the Instinct MI350X and MI355X on June 12, 2025 at Advancing AI 2025.

At GTC on March 16, 2026 NVIDIA expanded it to seven chips, the Vera CPU, Rubin GPU, NVLink 6 Switch, ConnectX-9 SuperNIC, BlueField-4 DPU, Spectrum-6 Ethernet switch and Groq 3 LPU, and declared them in full production.
In 2025, AMD acquired a team of AI hardware and software engineers from Untether AI along with compiler startup Brium.

market_signals.text: NVIDIA holds the crown with its mature CUDA ecosystem and dominant market share, but AMD’s Instinct line is rapidly closing the gap, offering greater memory capacity, open-source flexibility, and competitive performance at lower cost.
NVIDIA is the scale leader in AI infrastructure, and AMD is the focused challenger.
Morgan Stanley put NVIDIA at roughly 85% of AI processor revenue in March 2026, with custom ASICs above 10% and AMD below 5%.
NVIDIA holds ~80% of the AI accelerator market by revenue with $193.7B in FY2026 data center sales, versus AMD's estimated 5-7% share (~$7-8B in Instinct revenue).
The bigger structural threat to NVIDIA is custom silicon — Broadcom AI ASIC revenue hit $20B+ in FY2025 — not AMD.

risks.text: A key insight is that NVIDIA’s market lead maps directly to lower integration risk, while AMD’s value shows up when you have a narrower use case and the engineering discipline to stay inside it.

Prominent Chinese technology companies, including Alibaba and Baidu, are increasingly switching from Nvidia hardware to internally developed chips as U.S. export controls restrict the capabilities of Nvidia's offerings in the country.
Resumed shipments to China, following regulatory clearances for the H20 and other GPUs, are seen by names like Goldman Sachs as a potential $2 billion to $5 billion near-term revenue tailwind.
The risk that institutions remain underweight in the stock relative to S&P 500 benchmarks is also flagged as a potential headwind should sentiment shift or market leadership rotate away from AI.
Regulatory and competitive pressures in China continue to mount.

sources.title: AMD vs NVIDIA GPU: Which Performs Better for AI Workloads? - Fluence Cloud
sources.snippet: NVIDIA and AMD pursue the same goal—accelerating AI at scale—but their architectural strategies couldn’t be more different. NVIDIA builds around specialized AI accelerators like Tensor Cores and the Transformer Engine, fine-tuned for matrix-heavy deep learning tasks. AMD, by contrast, emphasizes raw compute density and superior memory bandwidth, relying on vast compute units and high-capacity memory stacks to drive performance across massive models. [...] AMD has returned to the AI race with strategic intent. Its Instinct series of accelerators—particularly the MI200, MI300X/MI325X, and upcoming MI350X—marks a serious challenge to NVIDIA’s grip on the data center market. These GPUs deliver exceptional memory capacity and bandwidth, crucial for handling today’s increasingly large models. [...] NVIDIA is the scale leader in AI infrastructure, and AMD is the focused challenger. That matters because market scale affects everything downstream: hardware availability, software investment, framework support, hiring, vendor partnerships, and the confidence you can have in a roadmap when you’re standardizing a platform.

sources.title: AMD vs NVIDIA AI GPU Market Share 2026: MI350X vs B200
sources.snippet:
NVIDIA holds ~80% of the AI accelerator market by revenue with $193.7B in FY2026 data center sales, versus AMD's estimated 5-7% share (~$7-8B in Instinct revenue). AMD's MI350X matches B200 on FP8 compute (4,600 TFLOPS) and exceeds it on memory (288GB vs 192GB HBM3E), but NVIDIA's software maturity delivers 50-55% MFU versus AMD's ~45%, preserving a real-world performance gap. The bigger structural threat to NVIDIA is custom silicon — Broadcom AI ASIC revenue hit $20B+ in FY2025 — not AMD. [...] NVIDIA holds approximately 80% of the AI accelerator market in 2026, with data center revenue reaching $193.7 billion in FY2026. AMD's Instinct GPU line generated an estimated $7–8 billion in 2025, capturing roughly 5–7% market share. However, the competitive landscape is more nuanced than a two-horse race: hyperscaler custom silicon (Google TPU, AWS Trainium, Broadcom ASICs) collectively represents a larger and faster-growing threat to NVIDIA than AMD does. The AI accelerator total addressable [...] The AI accelerator market is transitioning from NVIDIA monopoly to a three-tier competitive structure: NVIDIA retains 60–75% through 2028, AMD reaches 10–15% as the credible merchant silicon alternative, and custom silicon captures 15–25% concentrated in cloud-locked inference. All three can grow simultaneously because TAM is expanding from ~$200B to $500B+.

Both companies can win. Data as of April 2026.

sources.title: How Recent Developments Are Shaping the NVIDIA Investment Story
sources.snippet:
Several analysts, including Morgan Stanley with a target lift to $235, have cited persistent, outsized demand for NVIDIA's AI compute products. They applaud the accelerated ramps of Blackwell and GB300/B300 platforms as critical growth drivers.
 Bullish sentiment builds on NVIDIA's demonstrated execution and operational transparency. Analysts reward the company's cost control, expanding production capacity, and clear multi-year revenue guidance anchored by data center growth. [...] Nvidia's new RTX6000D AI chip, launched for the Chinese market, has received a muted reception. Many local firms are hesitant to commit, preferring to wait for the anticipated H20 or B30A models because of cost and performance concerns.
 The company is scaling back its DGX Cloud business, reducing direct competition with major cloud providers like AWS and instead placing greater emphasis on supporting its own internal research and development efforts. [...] Despite challenges, Nvidia remains active in expanding global AI infrastructure. The firm is entering new partnerships to invest in datacenter capacity in the UK with companies like CoreWeave and OpenAI. However, market volatility and skepticism about partner models persist.
